claims.text: High configurational entropy causes significant lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
Impeded dislocation motion enhances hardness and strength relative to similar lower-configurational-entropy alloys.
The proposed initial materials are single-phase, equiatomic high-entropy alloys with homogeneous atomic distributions.
Controlled heat treatments that promote ordering or segregation can reduce configurational entropy.
Atomic-size mismatch produces lattice distortions in the high-entropy alloy.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions create local stress fields.
Local stress fields produced by lattice distortion impede dislocation glide through a dislocation-pinning mechanism.
Dislocation pinning caused by lattice distortion is responsible for enhanced hardness and strength in high-entropy alloys.
High-entropy samples will have higher hardness than lower-entropy baseline samples.
High-entropy samples will have higher yield strength than lower-entropy baseline samples.
High-entropy samples will exhibit greater X-ray diffraction peak broadening than lower-entropy samples.
Greater X-ray diffraction peak broadening is indicative of increased lattice strain.
The proposed behavior is limited to single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloys in which lattice distortion is the dominant strengthening mechanism.
The proposed relationship may not apply when precipitation or grain-boundary strengthening is significant.
The magnitude of hardness and yield-strength enhancement depends on alloy composition and processing.
Local chemical ordering may influence mechanical behavior in addition to lattice distortion.

contradictions.description: The lower-entropy baseline may be produced by promoting segregation, while the stated testing conditions require homogeneous samples without secondary phases. Segregation would undermine that control and could introduce composition gradients or additional phases.

The hypothesis attributes lattice distortion to configurational entropy, whereas the structural mediator attributes it to atomic-size mismatch. The relationship between these two proposed causes is not resolved, making the governing variable ambiguous.
